articles.title: You've heard of quiet quitting. What about a quiet divorce?
articles.summary: Marriages don't always end with in-your-face blowout fights. Some fizzle slowly and silently over time, in what's known as a quiet divorce.
articles.body:
On paper, Amanda Thomas got divorced in 2025. But if you ask her, her marriage really ended two years earlier.

Their 20 years together didn't unravel from one dramatic fallout. For a long time, there was still love. There was stability, too: two kids, a house and a husband with a steady career. There was no single night she could point to and say, That's when I fell out of love.

But Thomas, now 42 and living in Washington, D.C., had started to feel like she was living the marriage alone.

Practical tips for a healthier, happier life. Sign up for free

She planned their date nights. She handled the chores, assembled the furniture and fixed things around the house. He seemed to find time for work, business and friends. For her, there was less.

At first, she still believed things could get better. She brought up what was bothering her and even looked for marriage counselors. Her husband would claim he "heard" her concerns, she recalled, or brush her off for "nagging." Either way, the result for more than a decade was the same: no change.

Eventually, she stopped giving more than she was getting. She quit asking for what she needed to feel loved and stopped expecting to get it. The difficult conversations disappeared. So did the idea that the marriage was worth fighting for.

It's not that she stopped caring, she said. "I just stopped taking responsibility for managing the health of the relationship."

Over time, her resentment dulled. The neglect stung less. She adjusted to her husband's emotional absence rather than expecting him to fill it. And while she wouldn't walk out the door for another two years, in a way she had already left.

In other words, she quietly quit her marriage.

What does it mean to quiet quit a marriage?

Much like the workplace version — doing the bare minimum to avoid getting fired — quiet quitting a marriage, or a "quiet divorce," happens when one or both people stay together on paper but check out emotionally.

In other words, "they're really not putting in effort toward the marriage," said Galena Rhoades, research professor at the University of Denver and director of the Institute for Relationship Science. "But they're not necessarily taking steps to end it."

Unlike an official decision to separate, there may be no single moment when someone decides they're giving up. As with Thomas, the withdrawal may be gradual, happening after years of trying — then becoming exhausted when nothing changes.

"I didn't think about divorce or separation," Thomas said. "That wasn't even on the top of my mind."

So why not just leave instead of living in limbo?

Often, it's practical. "Marriage is a financial agreement," said Molly Burrets, clinical psychologist and adjunct professor at the University of Southern California's Department of Marriage and Family Therapy. "We don't all have the independence to just leave a marriage any time that we want." There may be mortgages and child care costs , health insurance and shared bank accounts. Some parents stick it out for the kids, Burrets added. And for those in toxic or abusive situations, leaving can be dangerous.

Fear keeps people stuck, too. "What we often see is that they don't believe that the alternative life that they could have if they ended the marriage would be a good enough one," Rhoades explained. In this sense, pulling back can work as a trial run: a way to test life without your significant other before separating for good.

So where's the line between hitting a rough patch and heading for a quiet divorce? Here are the warning signs to look for.

You live like roommates or co-parents, not partners

One sign that Rhoades sees: The relationship feels less like a partnership and more like a business arrangement — two people managing a household but no longer sharing a life.

Maybe you talk all day, but it's almost entirely about logistics. Who's picking up the kids? Did you pay the electric bill? What's for dinner?

"They work well together. They're good at the business of life," Rhoades said. What's missing is everything else: curiosity about your partner's day, what's been on their mind, what they're stressed or worried or excited about.

Fighting isn't always bad . Sometimes it shows both partners, at the very least, are invested enough to speak up. Handled constructively, research suggests being able to engage in and resolve disagreements can even bring you closer.

The more concerning shift is when you quit caring enough to fight.

"The opposite of love is not anger," Burrets said. "The opposite of love is indifference," which can set in after years of letdowns. "When disappointment turns into resignation, that's when a quiet divorce often begins."

Physical affection fades, and you don't really miss it

A dry spell, on its own, doesn't mean a marriage is in trouble. But, according to Rhoades, physical intimacy is part of what makes a romantic relationship feel romantic for many couples.

And it's not just about having less sex. Maybe you stop kissing each other goodbye, reaching for their hand, sitting close together on the couch or grazing their shoulder as you pass in the kitchen.

"Again, those are things that you're only doing with your spouse," Rhoades said. "So when they start to fall away, it can be a sign that other things are shifting."

You start building a life that doesn't include your partner

At some point, Thomas saw how one-sided her marriage had become. "I remember having a moment where I realized, 'Oh my gosh, I'm putting all this energy into saving this,'" she recalled.

So, she gave up on asking, on hoping, on waiting for her husband to show up. Instead, she learned to depend on friends to give her the care and connection she had been missing.

"My girlfriends, they gave that to me tenfold," Thomas said. "And I didn't have to do anything for it."

It was a relief to feel so cared for easily, and that's what makes this shift so easy to miss, Burrets said. Slowly, people around you take over the roles your spouse should have: A colleague now hears the funny stories from your workout class; your friends get the doctor's appointment updates; your sister is your plus-one at parties.

Little by little, the marriage goes from essential to optional. And while having a life outside of your relationship is healthy, "when the distance no longer is really bothering you, that is a sign that you quietly quit your marriage," Burrets explained.

If you're the one who's quiet quitting, the first step is to stop running on autopilot and be honest about your needs.

"Get serious with yourself about where you are, what the factors are and if there's anything that is salvageable in the marriage before you take any moves to end it," Rhoades suggested.

That means answering uncomfortable questions: Am I staying because I want to, or because leaving feels scary, complicated or expensive? If my partner did everything I've been asking for, would that be enough? Am I willing to change, too, or am I already done?

A therapist can help you sort through those questions. But eventually, your partner should be a part of the conversation — which can be difficult if you've spent months or years believing there's no point.

For example, you might start with: "I've been feeling disconnected for a while, and I'm not sure where we stand anymore. Can we talk?" Or, if part of you sees potential, skip the vague "try harder" and get specific: "I'd like us to have one night a week together, no phones or TV, because I've been feeling neglected."

On the flip side, maybe you know you want out. Saying so can feel cruel, but Rhoades argues the opposite: "If the relationship is safe enough for honest discussion, clarity is usually healthier than maintaining a false sense of commitment."

If you're on the receiving end — sensing distance from your partner — try asking what's going on without accusing.

"Don't go in with a blaming mindset like, 'You're treating me this way," Burrets said. Lead with curiosity instead. For example, "You used to tell me about your day the second you walked in, and lately you don't. I miss that. Is something going on with us? Are we okay?"

You don't have to agree with their perspective, but focus on hearing what's underneath their disengagement before rushing to defend yourself. "If someone is quietly quitting the marriage, what that means is they've probably tried to get the problem solved with you over and over and over and haven't gotten the result that they want," Burrets said.

Repair, if you both want it, won't come from one heart-to-heart. Reversing the slow fade requires smaller, sustained efforts — and a lot of patience to rebuild trust and lost love.

And if it can't be saved, that can be an equally valuable answer. Two years of quiet gave Thomas what decades of begging and settling never did: Clarity.

"When that decision came to separate and divorce, I knew it was coming from a place of healing," she said. "So absolutely, I know and believe it was the best thing for me."

articles.body: KOLKATA: In an unprecedented incident in the heart of the city that resembled a medieval kangaroo court, an 18-year-old youth, his father, and his 19-year-old friend were reportedly severely assaulted, threatened at gunpoint, stripped, and forced to parade naked for more than 50 metres through a congested street in Sarsuna, south-west Kolkata, on Sunday evening by the family of the teenager’s minor girlfriend.The public humiliation unfolded after the youth was allegedly caught kissing his minor girlfriend near Khalpar Math in the Khudiram Pally area on Oct 25.Local outrage over the incident erupted into violence on Monday as enraged residents vandalised the house of the prime suspects and confronted the police over alleged delays in handling the case and arresting all the accused.The police denied any delay, insisting that three persons had been arrested so far, including the parents of the 13-year-old girl and her maternal uncle.According to eyewitnesses, the girl’s family had opposed the romantic relationship from the outset. The situation escalated dramatically when an associate of the girl’s relative spotted the couple together. The youth and his friend were dragged to the girl’s residence, locked inside a room, and assaulted by her father and maternal uncle.The girl’s family then summoned the youth’s father to the house, where the assault continued. The victim’s father alleged that he was also threatened with death.“They called me over, confined the three of us, and then severely assaulted me while many people were present. Later, they seemed to think that if they kept beating us like that, we might die. Then they gave me a choice: ‘Kill your son. If you don’t use a gun, stab him with a knife.’ The girl’s mother said it would not be that easy. She said she would heat the knife on the gas stove and hand it to me so that I could thrust it into my son’s stomach. I had no choice but to agree to strip to save my son,” the youth’s father alleged.Area residents recounted that the assailants held firearms and threatened to kill anyone who attempted to intervene.“The 18-year-old youth’s father was given three choices: shoot his son, stab him, or make him walk naked. They had guns in their hands and kept telling others to shoot. When we protested, they threatened us too, saying, ‘Get out of here, or we’ll open fire.’ Later, the boy’s father told us that this was the only way he could save his son,” claimed Arnab Saha, a local resident.“The 18-year-old victim had gone to meet the 13-year-old girl along with his 19-year-old friend near Khalpar Math in Sarsuna. While talking, the youth allegedly kissed her, which was witnessed by an associate of the girl’s uncle. He informed the girl’s maternal uncle and father, who then brought both boys to their house in Khudiram Pally. There, they assaulted the two boys and instructed the youth to call his father. In the meantime, the maternal uncle called three to four of his friends to the residence. When the youth’s father arrived, they assaulted him as well and threatened to kill them with a gun if they did not parade naked. They then forced the three of them to parade naked for about 50 metres in the lane outside,” said Additional CP (Crime) Kunal Aggarwal.Based on the complaint filed by the young man’s father, Sarsuna police station registered a case under sections pertaining to attempted murder (109), gang assault (118(i)), severe bodily harm (117(2)), illegal confinement (127(2)), extortion (356(2)), criminal intimidation (351(3)), abduction (140(3)) and organised crime (3(5)), along with relevant sections of the Arms Act for possessing unlicensed firearms.“The main accused—the parents of the girl and her maternal uncle—have been arrested. Raids are ongoing to apprehend the remaining accused. The medical examination of the young victims has been completed. They alleged that they were threatened at gunpoint to undress; however, no weapons have been recovered so far. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Election Commission on Monday filed a counter-affidavit in the Supreme Court defending its functioning and the conduct of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. articles.body: Vanessa Trump, the former wife of Donald Trump Jr., has opened up about the early symptoms of her breast cancer, revealing that extreme fatigue was one of the first signs she experienced months before her diagnosis. The 48-year-old, who is now cancer-free, shared details of her diagnosis, treatment and recovery during a recent interview with her daughter, Kai Trump, and Dr Nicole Saphier for Breast Cancer Awareness Month.Vanessa revealed that she had been feeling unusually exhausted for around six months before learning that she had breast cancer. She recalled struggling with fatigue even while carrying out simple everyday activities, such as making a trip to Starbucks.In the interview shared on Saturday, she explained that fatigue can be difficult to identify as a warning sign because it can easily be mistaken for the exhaustion that comes with motherhood and everyday responsibilities.Vanessa also revealed that her latest MRI results came back clear, offering reassurance following her treatment. Her account highlights the importance of paying attention to unusual changes in the body, even when the symptoms may appear routine.Vanessa Trump opens up about breast cancer treatmentVanessa offered a rare insight into her treatment for invasive ductal carcinoma, a type of breast cancer that begins in the milk ducts and spreads into surrounding breast tissue.She underwent a lumpectomy, a surgical procedure in which a tumour and a small margin of surrounding healthy tissue are removed. She also underwent three courses of radiation treatment as part of her cancer care.Vanessa further revealed that her cancer was attributed to environmental factors rather than genetic causes. Moving forward, she will undergo regular scans three to four times a year for the next five to 10 years to monitor her health.Vanessa Trump shares emotional message about her recoveryVanessa took to Instagram on Sunday to promote the interview, reflecting on what she described as a long and challenging journey with the disease.In her post, she expressed gratitude for the love and support she received from her family and those close to her during the difficult period. She also used the opportunity to encourage others to prioritise their health and undergo regular screenings.Vanessa wrote that she hoped sharing her experience would encourage people to schedule their screenings and understand the importance of early detection. She also disclosed that she had undergone a procedure.In June, Vanessa shared an update on her recovery, revealing that she had spent four weeks recuperating from surgery. articles.summary: Leanne Gregory of Nottinghamshire, England, was swept away by a strong current off North Bimini Island while trying to rescue her two sons during a family snorkeling trip.
articles.body: A 36-year-old mother on a family snorkeling excursion in the Bahamas recently died while trying to save her two sons from a strong current, authorities said. The victim was identified as Leanne Gregory, 36, of Nottinghamshire, England, according to The Telegraph. The drowning, which took place on North Bimini Island, was announced by Bahamian authorities last Tuesday. THOUSANDS BOOKED TROPICAL BAHAMAS CRUISE AND ENDED UP IN FREEZING CANADA INSTEAD The Royal Bahamas Police Force said that around 10 a.m. Tuesday, officers at the Alice Town Police Station were alerted to an unresponsive woman at the North Bimini Ferry Dock. The woman had been snorkeling with her husband and two sons when a "strong current" swept the children away, according to the statement. "In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away," police said in a statement. "She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered." Both children survived the incident, according to The Telegraph. NURSE IMPALED BY POLE DURING HIKE FORCED TO TREK 10 MILES FOR HELP: 'A FREAK THING' By the time officers arrived, they were told the woman had been transported to a clinic and pronounced dead by a local doctor "despite efforts to save her life," the report added. Authorities added that foul play "is not suspected at this time." "An autopsy will be conducted to assist in determining the exact cause of death," the report added. In a Facebook tribute, Gregory's husband, Nathan, called his wife of 22 years his "childhood sweetheart" and "soulmate," according to the BBC. The outlet reported that on a GoFundMe page, he said she held onto one of their sons until he was rescued, but she "didn't have the energy to save herself." "My boys had to witness something nobody should ever have to see of any age, but they know [their mom] died an absolute hero," Nathan Gregory said. But the waters were too rough and choppy for her." Gregory's mother-in-law told The Telegraph the couple were school sweethearts who had been together for over 20 years. articles.title: GORDON SONDLAND: France is burning, Europe's broke, and the revolution it really needs isn't violent
articles.summary: A former U.S. ambassador to the EU explains how excessive regulation and rigid labor markets fuel Europe's protests over rising living costs.
articles.body: Europe is in the streets. From Paris to Brussels, Milan to Lisbon, hundreds of thousands of citizens are protesting rising living costs, stagnant wages, unaffordable housing and deteriorating public services. In France, demonstrations have descended into burning barricades, looted businesses, and attacks on public buildings. Elsewhere, students, workers and frustrated families are demanding that their governments deliver the prosperity and security they have long promised. Most protesters are peaceful, but the unrest reflects a growing anxiety that Europe’s economic and social model is no longer delivering. The immediate grievances vary, but the underlying problem is more profound: too many European economies have become better at protecting yesterday’s arrangements than creating tomorrow’s opportunities. Excessive regulation, rigid labor structures, fragmented capital markets, and slow decision-making constrain the growth necessary to sustain Europe’s generous social promises. Europe has not run out of talent. It has made it unnecessarily difficult for talent to flourish. Having served as the U.S. ambassador to the EU, I have heard this firsthand from executives running the American operations of major European companies, particularly in Silicon Valley. Their message is remarkably consistent: they simply cannot innovate in Europe the way they can in the United States. These are Europeans describing the limitations of their own economic environment. They come to America because our ecosystem allows them to move faster, attract capital, take risks, recruit talent, and turn promising ideas into commercially successful businesses. FROM ARRESTS TO CRACKDOWNS, HOW EUROPE’S LEADERS ARE RESPONDING AS PROTESTS ROCK THE CONTINENT Think about the implications. Europe has extraordinary universities, brilliant engineers, world-class scientists, and sophisticated corporations. Yet many of those same corporations look to America when they want to push the boundaries of innovation. The problem is not imagination. It is an economic and regulatory structure that too often suffocates imagination before it can become commercial reality. There is another uncomfortable dimension to Europe’s predicament. For decades, the United States provided the military security umbrella under which European governments could devote comparatively modest resources to their own defense. While American taxpayers financed enormous military capabilities, many European countries concentrated more of their resources on generous pensions, health care, social benefits, and other domestic priorities. FRENCH CEO WARNS 'PURELY CHAOTIC' RIOTS PROVE THE COUNTRY HAS REACHED THE 'DEAD END OF SOCIALISM' Imagine if European governments had been required to spend 4% or 5% of GDP on defense throughout the past three decades. Would their social safety nets look anything like they do today? Perhaps Europeans would still have chosen extensive benefits, shorter workweeks and lengthy vacations. But those arrangements would have required far more difficult fiscal choices involving taxes, borrowing, spending and economic growth. American military power did not create Europe’s welfare state, but it helped make that welfare state easier to afford. HUNGARY AND POLAND DEFEND TOUGH MIGRATION POLICIES AS FRANCE REELS FROM VIOLENT UNREST The American security guarantee may also have distorted European perceptions of the threats themselves. When someone else bears much of the cost of protecting you, it becomes easier to discount the danger. Why acknowledge the full threat posed by Russia if doing so means telling voters they must sacrifice cherished benefits to purchase tanks, aircraft and missiles? Far easier for Europeans to conclude that Washington is exaggerating the danger, let America spend the money, and enjoy another three-hour lunch. Poland and the Baltic states have generally viewed Russia differently. But across much of Western Europe, American protection made strategic complacency easier to sustain. Now the defense bill is coming due. President Trump has pressed NATO allies to assume greater responsibility for their own security, and European governments have committed to substantially higher defense spending. Those commitments arrive just as their economies struggle to generate the growth necessary to finance them. FROM ARRESTS TO CRACKDOWNS, HOW EUROPE’S LEADERS ARE RESPONDING AS PROTESTS ROCK THE CONTINENT Europe needs an immediate regulatory reset, more integrated capital markets, flexible labor arrangements, faster permitting, affordable energy and an environment in which entrepreneurs can build global companies without crossing the Atlantic. Estonia’s digital government, Denmark’s labor flexibility, Ireland’s technology investment and Poland’s industrial development offer useful examples. What Europe lacks is not another commission or another report. It needs political leaders willing to confront the bureaucracies, vested interests and institutional inertia that prevent meaningful reform. Which brings us to America. We have our own protests, riots, economic inequalities, political dysfunction, and government bureaucracy. We are far from perfect, and we should never pretend otherwise. Millions of Americans struggle with housing costs, health care, education, and the fear that their children may not enjoy the opportunities they once expected. We have communities that feel abandoned, institutions that have lost public trust and political divisions that sometimes seem impossible to bridge. But America’s greatest strength has never been perfection. It is our extraordinary capacity for reinvention. Our system is built around the possibility of constant change. We experiment, fail, learn, improve and try again. Yesterday’s conventional wisdom becomes tomorrow’s obsolete business model. New companies challenge established giants. New technologies disrupt entire industries. Every generation has the opportunity to create something that did not exist before. That process can be messy, disruptive, and sometimes deeply unfair. But it creates something indispensable to a successful society: the belief that tomorrow can be better than today, and that individuals have the power to help make it so. This is the essential difference between American economic dynamism and the more rigid structures that constrain much of Europe. Our system does not guarantee success. It preserves the possibility of extraordinary success, and it gives people repeated opportunities to pursue it. COULD FRANCE'S RIOTS HAPPEN HERE? EXPERTS SEE PARALLELS IN SOCIALISM, IMMIGRATION — AND KEY DIFFERENCES Critics of American wealth inequality frequently point to our growing number of billionaires, and perhaps someday a trillionaire, as evidence of a system gone wrong. But the mere existence of extraordinary fortunes misses a fundamental point. The question is not simply how much wealth the richest American has accumulated. It is whether the next American, starting with little more than an idea, talent and determination, has a genuine opportunity to build something extraordinary. I want to wake up every morning believing the sky is the limit. I want every American to have that same opportunity. Not a government-imposed ceiling on ambition, not a predetermined limit on success, and not a tax system designed to punish exceptional achievement simply because it is exceptional. Why take the risk, invest the capital, work the extra hours or pursue the seemingly impossible if government has already decided how much success is enough? AMERICANS WARNED ABOUT PARIS TRAVEL AFTER VIOLENCE, LOOTING AND TEAR GAS-FILLED STREETS None of this means ignoring inequality. An economy in which wealth and power become permanently concentrated, established businesses suppress competition and children born into poverty have little realistic prospect of advancement would betray the very principles that make American capitalism work. Government has an essential role in enforcing the rule of law, protecting competition, providing education, maintaining a functioning safety net and ensuring that opportunity is not reserved for those who already possess wealth or influence. But there is an enormous difference between government creating the conditions for opportunity and government attempting to dictate economic outcomes. America should respond to Europe’s difficulties with neither arrogance nor indifference. A prosperous, innovative and militarily capable Europe is essential to our own security and economic interests. We should encourage European reform, welcome European investment and insist that our allies assume a greater share of their defense responsibilities. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION At home, however, we must be careful not to import the very economic rigidities Europe is struggling to escape. We should resist the temptation to address every imperfection with another layer of regulation, another barrier to investment or another policy that makes entrepreneurship less rewarding. We should instead ask a simpler question of every major economic policy: Does this make it easier or harder for Americans to work, invest, innovate, start businesses, change careers and recover from failure? And we must make sure that the promise of advancement remains credible. That means better schools, affordable housing, competitive markets, access to capital, effective public institutions and opportunities extending far beyond a handful of prosperous technology centers. America’s protests remind us that economic growth alone cannot sustain public confidence if too many citizens believe the system is closed to them. Peaceful dissent must be protected, violence must be rejected and legitimate grievances must be addressed. A dynamic economy cannot remain politically stable if large portions of its population lose faith in their ability to participate in its success. The answer to inequality is not to suppress exceptional outcomes. It is to prevent inequality from becoming permanent exclusion. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The American dream was never a guarantee that everyone would become wealthy. It was the conviction that nobody’s future had to be dictated by the circumstances of their birth. The measure of a successful society is not how effectively it limits the fortunes of those at the top, but how convincingly it keeps the door open for those who aspire to join them. Europe’s unrest should serve as a warning about what happens when expectations grow faster than the economy’s capacity to fulfill them, and when political institutions become better at protecting yesterday’s arrangements than creating tomorrow’s opportunities. America’s greatest asset is not the wealth it has already accumulated. It is the wealth, discoveries, industries and opportunities that have yet to be created. Europe needs to rediscover economic possibility. America needs to protect it. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM AMB. GORDON SONDLAND

articles.title: Ronnie James Dio cancer fund has raised more than $2 million since his death, backing research into early detection and treatment of prostate, colon and stomach cancers
articles.summary: Ronnie James Dio Cancer Fund donations have passed $2 million since the rock singer's death, giving his name a lasting role in medical research.
articles.body: Ronnie James Dio Cancer Fund donations have passed $2 million since the rock singer's death, giving his name a lasting role in medical research. The Ronnie James Dio Stand Up and Shout Cancer Fund is privately funded, with income from annual events and direct support from fans worldwide. Its money backs scientific institutions and their research, alongside education work aimed at cancer, from early detection and prevention through to treatment. Based in Studio City, California, the charity directs gifts of every size, from ticket sales to direct online donations, towards a single purpose, better tools for finding and treating cancer.Funding research that spots prostate, colon and stomach cancers earlier and guides treatmentAccording to the Dio Cancer Fund website, the charity concentrates on three cancers that are prostate, colon and stomach. It says it has spent the past ten years supporting scientific institutions that work with cutting-edge technology. Researchers use genetics and precise genetic information to build tools that identify cancer cells, which in turn helps doctors weigh up the treatment options open to a patient. The emphasis is on giving clinicians clearer evidence before they decide how to proceed.How a singer's death from stomach cancer grew into a charity backed by fans and brandsDio, a former member of Black Sabbath, died of gastric cancer in 2010, Billboard has reported. The charity that carries his name was formed in his honour and now draws support well beyond the music world. Its website lists partners and sponsors including DW Drums, Harley Owners Group, Glendale Harley Davidson, Law Tigers, Mountain Valley and Western Bagel, alongside Clair, CAT Entertainment Services and several food and drink brands.Bowl for Ronnie, the celebrity bowling night that keeps raising money for cancer researchA signature fundraiser is Bowl for Ronnie, a celebrity bowling party. Billboard reports that Sirius XM host Eddie Trunk has hosted the event at Pinz Bowling Centre, where a raffle of prizes and memorabilia runs alongside the tournament. Past line-ups have featured Tom Morello, Jack Black, Geezer Butler, Sebastian Bach and Richie Sambora. articles.title: A driver headed home to Alabama took a wrong turn in Georgia and spotted a house on fire, then rushed inside to wake a sleeping family of 14; the couple say they have fostered more than 500 children over 15 years
articles.summary: A driver travelling home to Alabama took a wrong turn along a Georgia highway, leading to the rescue of a sleeping family of 14 moments before their house
articles.body: A driver travelling home to Alabama took a wrong turn along a Georgia highway, leading to the rescue of a sleeping family of 14 moments before their house was engulfed by flames. The driver, identified by the family as a motorist named Mr Casey, was traveling with his son south of Lyerly, Georgia, just before midnight on Saturday, 17 October. Guided off his route by a GPS navigation error onto Highway 114, he reached the crest of a hill and saw flames spreading across a residential property. Instead of continuing on his journey, Mr Casey drove towards the burning structure, ran inside, and alerted the household. All 14 residents, including two adults, 11 children, and one grandchild, escaped the blaze unharmed.Late-night rescue on Highway 114The home belonged to James and Larita Burke, who were asleep alongside their family when the fire broke out. According to reports by local news outlet Local 3 News and reporting carried by Hoodline, Mr Casey entered the house to rouse the sleeping family and assisted in bringing all 12 children out of the structure to safety. He also remained on the scene to help guide emergency services to the rural location. Larita Burke spoke about how narrow the margin of survival was for her family that night. "If it had been another five minutes, it would've been a different situation," Larita Burke told KKTV. "We wouldn't have made it." Her husband, James Burke, explained that the driver felt compelled to follow the unfamiliar road after seeing the glow from the top of the hill. "He said that he knew that something kept bringing him down our road," James Burke said in an interview with 11Alive News. "When he saw the fire from the top of the hill, he knew he had to take action."Legacy of care for hundreds of childrenThe Burkes have dedicated much of their lives to child welfare in their local community. Over the past 15 years, the couple has fostered more than 500 children, providing temporary care and shelter to young people in need. Although the family survived without injury, the fire destroyed the home and all of their personal belongings. According to Local 3 News, the building was declared a total loss by emergency responders. Despite the destruction of their property, the family expressed gratitude that everyone escaped safely. Larita Burke emphasized that preserving life was the only outcome that truly mattered, stating in broadcast coverage by Local 3 News that "all our babies made it out."Community support and cause of the fireIn the days following the incident, neighbours and regional organizations mobilized to assist the displaced family with clothing, temporary shelter, and essential supplies. "It's overwhelming how much, immediately, people called to ask, 'Hey, what do you need? What can we do?'" James and Larita Burke told 11Alive News. "There are so many wonderful people in this community that have reached out. I didn't realize this county was as wonderful as it was until something like this happened." The Burkes confirmed that they intend to rebuild their home on the site and plan to resume fostering children once permanent housing is established. The Chattooga County Sheriff's Office reported that the cause of the fire remains under investigation, with official determinations pending further forensic examination of the site.You use AI every day. articles.title: Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 employees in India, US, UK and Canada; HR head Amy Coleman tells staff: Eligible employees will receive an email with...
articles.summary: Microsoft is offering buyouts to around 60,000 employees across India, the US, the UK and Canada, its second voluntary exit programme this year and a much
articles.body: Microsoft is offering buyouts to around 60,000 employees across India, the US, the UK and Canada, its second voluntary exit programme this year and a much wider one than the first. Announced on Monday in a memo from Chief People Officer Amy Coleman, the Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) covers more than a quarter of the company's roughly 223,000 employees. It reaches up to level 70 on Microsoft's internal scale, which takes in general managers and some staff with vice president titles, though not corporate vice presidents.Unlike the retirement buyout Microsoft ran earlier this year, this one has no age or tenure cut-off, and performance plays no part in who qualifies. Eligible employees will get an email with their individual terms within hours. They have until the first week of December to decide, and those who accept will leave at the end of the year."This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support," Coleman wrote. It also gives participating organisations "another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs," she added.Microsoft's voluntary exit offer pays out like its standard severanceThe package matches Microsoft's standard severance. That means base pay linked to tenure and level, continued stock vesting, healthcare for a fixed period and career transition support. What it leaves out is the extended healthcare that made the retirement programme an easy yes for many long-serving staff.Severance in Microsoft's US layoffs earlier this year started at 60 days of base pay and went up to 39 weeks for most employees. Staff at level 64 and below got a week of base pay for every six months of service, while levels 65 to 67 got two weeks.Not every team is in. Business leaders decide whether their groups participate, and sales is sitting this one out. Marketing, commercial business, security, and discovery and quantum teams are excluded too, according to people familiar with the matter. Copilot, CoreAI, Windows + Devices, Xbox, finance and HR are among those taking part, while Cloud + AI and Microsoft AI are partially in.Buyouts now sit alongside layoffs in Microsoft's AI-era job cutsThe VEO builds on the Voluntary Retirement Program from this spring, the first in Microsoft's history. That offer went to roughly 8,750 US employees at senior director level and below whose age and years at the company added up to at least 70. About 30% took it, and Microsoft booked a $900 million charge for it in April.The turnout helped shrink the layoffs that followed, Coleman said later. Microsoft still cut 4,800 jobs in July, about 2% of its workforce, and several hundred more in September, after cutting over 15,000 in 2025. Headcount stood at 223,000 on June 30, down from 228,000 a year earlier.The company is under pressure to hold down operating costs while it spends tens of billions on data centres and AI infrastructure. Still, Microsoft says the buyout is not a sign it needs fewer people, nor a replacement for layoffs, which remain on the table. It expects a much smaller share of employees to accept this time.Quarterly earnings on Wednesday could offer a first look at what the offer will cost. Coleman called the programme "new for us" in her memo, and said in July that Microsoft was studying whether voluntary exits could become a regular, even annual, fixture. How many of these 60,000 employees take the deal will likely settle that.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: A man said he was left "shocked" after being the victim of antisemitic abuse at Jewish wedding.
articles.body:
A Jewish man who was victim of antisemitic abuse after a man stormed into his brother's wedding reception has described his "fear" and "shock" that left him feeling nervous about attending large Jewish gatherings.

Jack Surpree, had been best man at the wedding at a hotel in Liverpool when he was confronted by Joseph Nixon, 43, who started shouting at guests in what a court heard was a "hate spree".

"In that moment all I could see was hatred and evil," Surpree said in a victim impact statement read to the court.

Nixon of Armagh, Northern Ireland, was given a community order at Liverpool Magistrate's Court on Monday.

Nixon had returned to the Adelphi Hotel in the early hours of 15 September last year when he confronted Surpree, the court heard.

Surpee said he had seen Nixon "storm" into the privately-hired hall.

"He decided to continue his hate spree," he said.

Surpree left his brother's wedding reception, in a function room of the hotel, with his teenage sister at about 12.45am and was in the reception area when he was approached by Nixon and another man, Louise Coe, prosecuting, said.

Nixon was said to have asked him whether he supported Palestine and then, after Surpree ignored him, whether he supported Israel.

The court heard Surpree then "clearly" heard him make an antisemitic comment.

In a statement, Mr Surpree said he went to take his phone out of his jacket pocket and saw the man's facial expression change, which made him "fear he was going to become violent" towards him and his sister.

He said the two men then entered the function room where he could hear "aggressive" shouts.

The incident was said to have lasted seven to eight minutes before Nixon was arrested.

In the victim impact statement Surpree said: "I remember feeling shocked. I had never been the victim of hate before that day."

Surpree said his parents had saved "for years" for the wedding and his sister-in-law told him she had waited "her whole life" for the day and did not "want it to be remembered like this".

He added: "He chose to target me because I am Jewish. He chose to bring hatred into what should have been one of the happiest days of my life."

He urged Nixon to educate himself and "make an effort to speak to Jewish people".

Simon Pook, defending, said at the time of the incident Nixon was under "serious and significant stress" as he was caring for his elderly parents, who later died, and his marriage was breaking down.

He said: "He has witnessed and experienced discrimination for being Irish and, second, for being Catholic."

He told the court Nixon, who works as a chef, had come to Liverpool for a break from stress and did not normally drink, but had been drinking at the time of the incident.

He said: "He is ashamed of the comments he made. He is ashamed of his conduct. That is not who he is and he has full empathy for Mr Surpree for the distress he has caused him."

Nixon was found guilty after a trial of racially or religiously aggravated intentional harassment.

Magistrates handed him an 18-month community order, with 300 hours of unpaid work, and ordered him to pay a £114 surcharge, £650 court costs and £150 compensation to Mr Surpree.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Five people were killed and one injured after a shooting at Hotel Bilas Inn in Guwahati’s Bora Service area around 9pm on Monday, with police suspecting that a property dispute over the hotel’s lease agreement triggered the attack.Guwahati Police Commissioner Partha Sarathi Mahanta said the accused, identified as Ghanakanta Gogoi, was apprehended within an hour of the incident. articles.title: Political battle intensifies within Labour over Rosebank oil field
articles.summary: Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra is urging the energy secretary to approve the controversial plans.
articles.body:
Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra is wading into the political battle which is intensifying over the Rosebank oil field.

He is making a direct appeal to Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to approve the plans to allow production to begin in the North Atlantic.

Environmentalists have long campaigned against the proposals for drilling in the UK's largest untapped oil field, 80 miles north-west of Shetland.

That the debate is now taking place within the Labour Party is a sign of the UK's recent journey on the politics of energy.

When Labour came to power in 2024, it was with a manifesto pledge not to allow any new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea.

A legal challenge thrust the future of the Jackdaw and Rosebank developments into the hands of the then-Energy Secretary, Ed Miliband.

At that point, senior offshore industry figures didn't hold out much hope of getting the go-ahead, given Miliband's deep commitment to renewable energy and his close political ties to Prime Minister Keir Starmer.

All that was before the outbreak of the war between the US, Israel and Iran, which closed the Strait of Hormuz and made an ongoing cost of living crisis even worse.

A new government under Andy Burnham entered 10 Downing Street with greater political freedom on the issue - and a new energy secretary to make the decisions.

Strictly speaking, Jackdaw and Rosebank aren't applications for new drilling licences, just the adjudication of existing ones.

But in political terms, the change of tone within Labour has been clear.

What had been an article of faith on energy has become something much more flexible.

It's a shift that's also plain to see within the SNP, with the Scottish government that once favoured a presumption against new oil and gas drilling now issuing a careful welcome to the Jackdaw announcement.

Last week, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh announced that production could begin on the Jackdaw gas field .

She said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, the project would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.

Environmentalists said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.

The UK government has always insisted that these decisions are part of a quasi-judicial process, judged on strict environmental criteria, not politics.

But as attention turns to Rosebank, the politics are seeping in.

Within hours of Jackdaw being granted approval, a briefing campaign began suggesting that Fahnbulleh was "minded" to reject Rosebank.

Now, in the week of the Budget, reports have suggested that Chancellor John Healey is in favour of approval.

Neither cabinet minister has given their view publicly, of course.

Fahnbulleh has insisted that the decision is "a regulatory process not a policy process," adding: "It sits heavy for such a big controversial decision because in the end only I can make it."

Even though she isn't looking for advice, the Scottish Labour leader is willing to offer it.

Marra is in Westminster meeting both Healey and Fahnbulleh in the run-up to the Budget on Wednesday.

Marra believes that on jobs and investment, the case for Rosebank is clear.

"I supported Jackdaw and Rosebank because I think they're really crucial for the Scottish economy, for employment, and for the public finances as well," he told me.

"We need to make sure that we're a country that people feel they can invest in.

"You've seen what's happened with Jackdaw in recent days - a real boost to the morale and the investment climate in the north east of Scotland."

He's also arguing for increased levies on banks in the Budget, to contribute towards the cost of help on the cost of living.

That second request looks set to be granted - which is likely why Marra feels able to make it publicly.

On Rosebank, we still can't say for sure how things will go.

But the fact this debate is even being had is itself a symbol of our new energy reality.

articles.title: Success story of startup Sagar Defence: From 150 sq ft workspace to leading provider of swarm boats to Navy
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A startup that started its operations from a tiny 150 sq ft workspace in Mumbai has now grown into a full-fledged defence company with major
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A startup that started its operations from a tiny 150 sq ft workspace in Mumbai has now grown into a full-fledged defence company with major R&D and manufacturing campuses in Pune and Andhra Pradesh. The success story of Sagar Defence, which was founded in 2015 by Capt Nikunj Parashar along with co-founders Mridul Babbar, Lakshay Dang, Saurabh Patil, and Ankit Kumar, is replete with failures, hard work and perseverance.While addressing a gathering at the Indian Navy’s ‘Swavlamban’ Naval Innovation and Indigenisation Seminar here as a guest speaker on Monday, Capt Parashar disclosed that he survived two heart attacks and a paralytic stroke and faced a lot of setbacks while struggling to make their company witness success. Sagar Defence is now a leading player for swarm boats, autonomous and unmanned weapons systems to the Indian armed forces, especially to the Indian Navy. Similar unmanned or swarm boats have been used by Iran and the US to attack each other and for surveillance purposes during the ongoing West Asia conflict.Under the Navy’s iDEX ‘SPRINT’ contract, the Pune-based company has now begun supplying 12 armed unmanned surface vessels (USVs)—including their signature ‘Matangi’ craft—to the Indian Navy. These high-speed, interceptor boats are equipped with 12.7mm stabilised remote-controlled gun stations, advanced electro-optical radar tracking, and anti-jamming GPS navigation to strike targets autonomously. They can be used as an unmanned boat for surveillance and offensive operations in shallow waters or can even carry marine commandos (Marcos) for special operations. Some of these boats have also been deployed at the Pangong Tso lake in eastern Ladakh by the Army for patrolling.Sagar Defence also produces custom multi-payload quadcopters and hexacopters such as Spectre and Varuna series and Maritime Spotter Drone designed to land on moving warships. The Indian company has also partnered with Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) to co-develop and introduce the "Point Blank" precision strike missile to India. This is a hand-launched, vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) system that acts as a loitering munition for high-speed precision strikes.At the ‘Swavlamban’ naval exhibition at Manekshaw Centre, another startup Zen technologies displayed their autonomous surface vessel prototype, which is a multirole and networked unmanned craft that can be used for surveillance, fire support, anti-submarine warfare and for other naval missions. C14 unveiled its Tandav autonomous, modular USV platform and also AquaScan, an AI vision device that can be used by divers for underwater vision. A C14 representative said the Navy has shown interest in its AqaScan and plans to buy it.Space startup Galaxeye is offering the Navy a satellite-based solution for keeping an eye on hostile or shadow vessels that loiter around in Indian waters. “Besides wide-area monitoring, night-time and adverse weather monitoring, we are ready to offer a solution to the Navy to detect an unknown or unidentified vessel that is loitering around in the Indian waters from space itself. Our satellite-based system can even provide the entire data or history of that shadow vessel with a click of the mouse,” Aarav Saexna, forward deployed engineer of Galaxeye, told TOI.

articles.title: Maxxing selected as Dictionary.com word of the year
articles.summary: "Whatever we're doing, we want to push it further," said an expert on why Americans are embracing the term, which is short for maximising.
articles.body:
Americans have gone all in on "maxxing", making it the 2026 Word of the Year for Dictionary.com.

Short for maximising, the term "can be used on its own or added to the end of any word to convey you're doing something to the fullest or optimizing it as much as possible", Dictionary.com said in a statement.

It's a major departure from two years ago, when the site, after analysing US social media trends, news stories, and search data, chose demure as word of the year. Last year's was "67".

"Maxxing is the linguistic manifestation of a culture increasingly preoccupied with getting the most out of everything," said Steve Johnson, director of lexicography for the Dictionary Media Group.

Digital media used "maxxing" nearly 19 times more in August 2026 compared to the 2025 monthly average, Dictionary.com found. The site also considered affordability, data centre, odyssey, and the shortened form of uncle, "unc", as potential words of the year.

On social media, many people in Generation Z and younger - those under 30 - post extensively about their maxxing efforts to achieve all sorts of perfection.

Influencers focused on fitness and wellness post about "proteinmaxxing" and "fibermaxxing". Those giving their full attention to improving sleep habits say they are "sleepmaxxing".

The influencer Clavicular has gained thousands of followers as he chronicles his extreme "looksmaxxing" - working to meet a set of prescribed criteria for attractiveness, with particular importance given to jawlines, eyes and physique.

"Whatever we're doing, we want to push it further," Johnson said. "But its expanding uses also reveal how people are responding to that impulse. Some embrace it. Some exaggerate it for laughs. Others subvert it entirely to describe stepping back from the relentless pursuit of more."

People were playing with the term - and idea - for decades before Clavicular started posting videos.

In the opening song for the 1990's television show The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, for example, Will Smith raps: "Chillin' out, maxin', relaxin' all cool."

articles.title: Texas couple lose possession of 70 acres after man's mother excluded him from her will; appeals court upholds eviction ruling involving property held by family for decades
articles.summary: A Texas couple who had been living on 70 acres of land they said had belonged to their family for decades have lost their fight to keep possession of the
articles.body: A Texas couple who had been living on 70 acres of land they said had belonged to their family for decades have lost their fight to keep possession of the property. William Dan Moss and his wife, Brenda Moss, had challenged an eviction order after a dispute that began with William being left out of his mother's will. A Texas appeals court ruled against the couple on Thursday, allowing the earlier eviction judgment to stand.The property is located in Sulphur Springs, Hopkins County. According to the details of the case available on Justia, William's mother had owned a share of the land, but when she died, her will specifically excluded him from inheriting her estate. William disagreed with that decision and took the matter to court. His challenge was unsuccessful, but the disagreement over the land did not end there.William later brought another case in an attempt to establish his claim to the property. That also failed. Meanwhile, Mark Lawrence, who represented a group known as the Garner Heir Group, wanted William and Brenda to leave the land. But Lawrence maintained that the group had never given the couple permission to occupy it.What followed was a series of court proceedings over who had the right to remain on the property. Although the couple repeatedly challenged the decisions against them, the courts ruled in favour of Lawrence.How the dispute over the 70 acres unfoldedThe first major setback for William came when he challenged his mother's will in a Hunt County court. The court rejected his claimHe then approached a district court in Hopkins County, this time seeking a ruling in his favour over the land itself. But that attempt ended with another judgment against him. William did not appeal the decision.After these proceedings, Lawrence formally asked the couple to vacate the property. When they remained there, he filed an eviction case, saying that neither William nor Brenda had received permission from the Garner Heir Group to occupy the land.The local justice court agreed with Lawrence and awarded him possession. The Mosses then appealed to the Hopkins County Court at Law.The couple represented themselves during the proceedings and chose to have a jury hear the case. On March 9, both sides presented their arguments. But again, the jury decided that the Garner Heir Group had the stronger right to possess the property. The Mosses continued their challenge, taking the dispute to the Sixth Court of Appeals in Texas.Why the couple say the eviction was wrongThe couple's main argument was that the lower courts should not have ordered them to leave without first deciding who legally owned the land.They also pointed out that they were not tenants of Lawrence. In their view, the absence of a landlord-tenant relationship meant the eviction case should not have proceeded.The appeals court disagreed on both points. It explained that not every eviction involves a tenant and a landlord. Texas law also allows proceedings against someone accused of occupying property without the necessary legal permission. In such cases, a tenancy agreement is not required.The judges also considered the couple's argument about ownership. They found that the earlier district court case had already dealt with William's claim to the property. Since that case had ended in a final judgment against him, the eviction court did not need to settle the ownership question again.There was another attempt by the couple to challenge the previous decisions. Shortly before the March jury trial, they had submitted a one-page document seeking a review of earlier court judgments.But the appeals court found problems with that filing. It contained no specific claims or legal arguments and had not been submitted to the court that issued the original judgment. The trial court had also rejected it after the jury proceedings.Why the final challenge also failedThe Mosses raised another objection concerning the Garner Heir Group. They argued that it was not a legally recognised entity and therefore could not bring a lawsuit or appoint Lawrence to represent it.However, the appeals court found that the couple had not properly raised this objection during the earlier trial. Under the applicable rules, a challenge to someone's legal authority to bring a case must be made through the required court filing. The judges found no record of the Mosses having done so.With both arguments rejected, the Sixth Court of Appeals upheld the judgment granting possession of the 70 acres to Lawrence on behalf of the Garner Heir Group.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2014, Chris Hemsworth bought a 10-acre Australian estate for A$7 million and demolished its eight-bedroom house; by 2026, the rebuilt compound had a 50-metre pool, tennis court and dirt-bike track
articles.summary: Hollywood actor Chris Hemsworth and his wife, Elsa Pataky, bought a 4.2-hectare coastal property near Byron Bay, Australia, for A$7 million in 2014,
articles.body: Hollywood actor Chris Hemsworth and his wife, Elsa Pataky, bought a 4.2-hectare coastal property near Byron Bay, Australia, for A$7 million in 2014, demolished its eight-bedroom Balinese-style residence and replaced it with a sprawling modern mansion featuring a 50-metre rooftop infinity pool. More than a decade later, a report published in 2026 has drawn attention to further recreational additions reportedly made to the compound, including a tennis court and a dirt-bike track, according to The Express Gazette.The estate, located at Broken Head on the New South Wales coast, overlooks Seven Mile Beach and lies around 12 kilometres from Byron Bay. The 4.2-hectare property is equivalent to approximately 10.4 acres. The couple's decision to transform the site into a contemporary family home attracted considerable attention, with the scale of the construction becoming a talking point among local residents.From a Balinese-style resort to a modern mansionBefore Hemsworth acquired the land, the property was known as Kooeloah, a private resort with an eight-bedroom, 11-bathroom residence, a lagoon-style swimming pool and ocean views. The property had reportedly been offered for around A$15 million in 2011, but remained on the market before Hemsworth and Pataky bought it three years later for A$7 million.The couple decided against retaining the existing residence and instead pursued a complete redevelopment. They submitted a development application to Byron Shire Council in late 2016, which was approved in March 2017. Construction began later that year, and aerial photographs published in 2018 and 2019 documented the scale of the replacement structure.The redevelopment was substantial. The new home was designed with six bedrooms, a gym, steam room, media room, games room and expansive outdoor spaces. The rooftop infinity pool, measuring 50 metres, became one of the property's most widely reported features.According to realestate.com.au, construction costs were estimated at approximately A$8.8 million in 2019, while the completed estate was described at the time as a roughly A$20 million property. Later reporting in 2025 suggested that the home's value could have reached A$50 million, although such figures were estimates rather than confirmed sale prices.A pool, solar panels and an expansive outdoor settingThe pool was only one part of the property's transformation. The couple also installed hundreds of solar panels, commissioned artwork for the interior and incorporated extensive areas for outdoor recreation and family activities. In 2019, Hemsworth shared photographs of a large mural created by Indigenous Australian artist Otis Hope Carey. Titled Darrundang Gaagal, meaning "thanking the ocean", the work uses patterns associated with the ceremonial dancing of the Gumbaynggirr people and imagery representing the ocean's healing powers.The estate also gained a skateboard ramp, another feature documented in aerial photographs in late 2019. Its combination of contemporary architecture, leisure facilities and privacy helped turn the property into one of Australia's most recognisable celebrity homes. The scale of the redevelopment was not universally welcomed. Some Byron Bay residents criticised the building's size, comparing it to a shopping centre or a concrete palace. Others defended the project, pointing to the couple's approvals and use of local tradespeople.Tennis court and dirt-bike track reportedly addedA newer report published by The Express Gazette in 2026 says the property has gained additional recreational facilities, including a tennis court and a purpose-built dirt-bike track. The report refers to aerial images from late July 2026 and says planning documents put the tennis court's estimated cost at nearly A$150,000. It also suggests that the estate's value could now exceed A$75 million. However, that valuation has not been independently established, and the report's claims about the new amenities require corroboration from stronger sources, such as the underlying planning documents or independently verified aerial imagery.The additions, if confirmed, would extend the estate's existing emphasis on recreation and fitness. Hemsworth has spoken publicly about his interest in physical training, while the couple have shared occasional glimpses of their family life at the property. The home already includes a gym, spa, steam room and large outdoor areas. The newer facilities should not be confused with the original construction plans, which documented the six-bedroom house, rooftop infinity pool and other leisure spaces but did not establish the presence of a tennis court or dirt-bike track.Why the family chose Australia's east coastHemsworth and Pataky moved from Los Angeles to the Byron Bay region with their three children in 2014. The move reflected their preference for a quieter lifestyle away from the intense attention associated with Hollywood. Hemsworth has said that he feels less famous and more grounded in Byron Bay.The region has since become a destination for other high-profile residents, including members of the Hemsworth family. In 2025, realestate.com.au reported that Hemsworth's brother, Liam, had acquired nearby land and was planning a substantial home of his own.The family's property holdings have added to the area's profile, although the growth in local property values cannot be attributed to any single celebrity purchase alone.You use AI every day. articles.title: Trump administration illegally fired James Comey's daughter, judge rules
articles.summary: Maurene Comey believes she was let go from her job as a federal prosecutor because her father is the former FBI director.
articles.body:
The US justice department illegally fired Maurene Comey, the daughter of former Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) director James Comey, a federal judge has ruled.

Comey, who lost her job as a federal prosecutor in New York in July 2025, sued the government, arguing she was unlawfully fired because of her father, a critic of US President Donald Trump, and because of her perceived political affiliations.

Judge Jesse Furman ruled on Monday that the Trump administration must reinstate her and that she must be given back pay.

A spokesperson for the justice department said in a statement that it disagreed with the decision and "will appeal in due course".

In his ruling, Judge Furman said Comey's dismissal violated the US Constitution as well as his right to a fair legal process.

He said the US attorney general can fire federal prosecutors but only "in a particular manner and only for certain reasons".

Furman noted that in Comey's role, "she was assigned some of the country's highest profile cases and consistently received the highest accolades from supervisors and peers alike".

Comey has worked on cases against the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell, and hip-hop mogul Sean "Diddy" Combs, who was convicted on prostitution-related charges involving his two ex-girlfriends last year.

Furman ordered that Comey be given back pay from July until December 2025, when she accepted a new job.

In a statement, Comey's lawyers said: "This hard-earned victory belongs to Ms Comey, to all civil servants, and to all fighting for the rule of law."

Comey had previously said the only reason she was told about her firing was that it "came from Washington".

A complaint filed by her lawyers in September 2025 stated that they believed Comey had been fired "solely or substantially because her father is former FBI Director James B Comey, or because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs, or both".

The justice department said in court filings that the decision was made by former Attorney General Pam Bondi.

The Trump administration has twice brought charges against James Comey, including for allegedly lying to Congress, but that case was dismissed by a judge who said the prosecutor who brought the case was unlawfully appointed.

Earlier this year, the justice department charged Comey with knowingly and wilfully making a threat to take the life of, and to inflict bodily harm, on the president. He has denied any wrongdoing.

The case stems from a 2025 Instagram post shared by Comey that contained a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to read "86 47".

"Eighty-six" is a slang term for "get rid of", and prosecutors allege it encourages violence against Trump.

articles.title: H-1B visa holder from India arrested in Ohio on child pornography charges; faces 10 years in prison if convicted
articles.summary: 39-year-old Vimalesh Prem Kumar, an Indian national working in the US on H-1B visa, has been arrested by federal agents on charges alleging that he
articles.body: 39-year-old Vimalesh Prem Kumar, an Indian national working in the US on H-1B visa, has been arrested by federal agents on charges alleging that he accessed and downloaded child pornography. According to charging documents, cyber tips led agents to Kumar’s online accounts. Kumar allegedly viewed child pornography via Instagram, Twitter and Telegram and downloaded and shared the child sexual abuse material on Telegram.The uploaded child sexual abuse material allegedly included explicit images of a young girl next to a teddy bear and a young girl wearing sheer lingerie.“HSI special agents continue to leverage every tool at our disposal and our national footprint to identify and investigate predators who share horrendous and obscene images of children being abused,” said HSI Detroit acting Special Agent in Charge Jeremy Pierczynski. “Working in the U.S. as a foreign national is a privilege and violators that target the most vulnerable members of our community will be held fully accountable under the law.”Kumar is charged with possessing or accessing child pornography with the intent to view it, a federal crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison.Dominick S Gerace II, United States Attorney for the Southern District of Ohio; Jeremy Pierczynski, Acting Special Agent in Charge, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit; and officials with the Ohio Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Task Force announced the charges. articles.title: Rapper Macklemore begins Free Palestine tour after Ed Sheeran fallout
articles.summary: Proceeds from the tour, which begins in Dublin next month, will go to organisations supporting Palestinians, he says.
articles.body:
Macklemore has begun his Free Palestine tour in Dublin after Ed Sheeran's controversial decision to drop the rapper from his tour last month.

The American star is playing to a crowd of up to 13,000 at the city's 3Arena - and, hours before the sell-crowd show, had promised "many incredible surprise guests".

The artist - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - announced the tour days after being dropped from Sheeran's Loop Tour following pro-Palestinian comments he made onstage.

He was criticised by Jewish groups after saying "Free Palestine" at two concerts and making political speeches, including referring to the death toll from Israel's military action in Gaza as a genocide - a claim that Israel rejects.

Sheeran later stressed that the decision to drop Macklemore was made by his promoter , not by himself.

Macklemore has said that proceeds from his Free Palestine tour will go to organisations supporting Palestinians.

He will perform in Paris on Thursday and in London on Friday.

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 70,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Israel says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.

Tickets for the Dublin show sold out and dozens of concertgoers were queueing at the venue hours before the its doors were opened.

Some were dressed in Palestinian jerseys, had tied Palestinian and Irish flags to themselves, and many were wearing keffiyeh scarves, a symbol of Palestinian identity.

Vendors outside the arena sold Palestinian bucket hats and flags, as well as hats and flags with the logo of Irish rap trio Kneecap.

Nicola McCollough travelled with her daughter Lily Rose Murphy from Belfast for Lily Rose's first ever concert.

They both said they were happy Macklemore spoke out in support of Gaza.

"More people need to, if you have the platform, do it because not everybody has that kind of stage," said Nicola.

"I would speak about anything if I'm supportive of it," said Lily Rose.

Gillian Duffy also travelled from Cork with her son Joshua.

She said that if Macklemore had "put on 10 shows in Dublin, all 10 would have been filled".

"This is the hottest ticket because people want to be here, they really, really want to show their support," she said.

"You're going to hear [the chant] 'Free, free Palestine' all over Dublin tonight."

Jess O'Riordan travelled from Cork and it was "absolutely appalling" when he was "kicked off" Sheeran's tour.

"I wish we had more people out there that would use their platform the way he does," she added.

Why was Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran's tour?

The controversy began when Macklemore, performing as the opening act for Sheeran at a concert in New Jersey in early September, said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."

The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University in the US.

The lyrics are critical of Israel's military actions in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack.

After he was taken off the tour on 14 September, Macklemore accused stadium owners of rallying together to push him out.

He was also accused by billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric surrounding Israel and Gaza.

Sheeran said that the decision to drop Macklemore from his tour was made by concert promoter Messina Touring Group.

His early remarks led to all of his support acts to drop out of the tour in solidarity with Macklemore, and fans to express frustration.

Sheeran then addressed the controversy during the start of a gig in Philadelphia.

He said he had made "mistakes" handling the fallout, apologising to fans and taking a stand on the Israel-Gaza conflict, which he said was "a humanitarian issue".

He described the 7 October 2023 attacks as "horrific" and also called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable and disproportionate".

articles.title: Phalli’s rise in underworld from a peanut seller to narco king, held after 1,900km chase
articles.summary: Nagpur gangster Vishal “Phalli” Gupta, accused under MCOCA for narcotics and firing case, arrested in Rameswaram after 1,900km chase; MD network busted.
articles.body: Nagpur: A MCOCA accused facing multiple narcotics offences, 25-year-old gangster Vishal Gupta alias Phalli, was arrested from Rameswaram in Tamil Nadu on Saturday after being on the run for two months. He was tracked down with his girlfriend Sahali Pandhram, 1,900km away from his home turf.Police were on Gupta’s hot pursuit after the August 26 firing outside corporator Shubham Motghare’s home put him at the centre of a major organised-crime probe.Popularly known as Phalli as he would sell peanuts on a roadside handcart with his father outside a Wathoda beer bar, Gupta had a meteoric rise in Nagpur’s underworld with an absolute grip on the interstate mephedrone network.Sources said the family migrated from Uttar Pradesh two decades ago and over the years he joined local gangs, graduated from petty offences to serious crimes, and almost eliminated an aide.Police records list around 15 cases against him, including murder, attempt to murder, rape and assault. He was also held under preventive detention laws.With murders registered in 2016 and again in 2020, Phalli became a hardened criminal. After securing bail in a 2020 murder case, he allegedly expanded his MD trade, built a supply chain linking Nagpur with Rajasthan through Madhya Pradesh and Ujjain. In 2024, the crime branch nabbed him with three firearms, but he again returned to the trade once released.Phalli came under intense scrutiny after allegedly opening fire on Congress corporator Motghare’s residence at Shrawan Nagar on August 26. Investigators believe the attack stemmed from a bitter fallout as Phalli suspected Motghare of tipping off cops about his links with drug peddlers. After the shooting, Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act (MCOCA) was invoked against him.The breakthrough came on October 24 when crime branch unit led by senior inspector Vinayak Golhe raided a flat in Narendra Nagar and arrested five men and seized 1.405 kg MD, six mobile phones, Rs 3.44 lakh in cash, a car, four two-wheelers and other material pegged at Rs 1.54 crore. A sixth accused was later held. Police alleged Phalli coordinated the consignment from his hideout and sent an advance of Rs 15 lakh through his network.“We are looking at backward and forward linkages. Already facing MCOCA, Phalli may face another case under the stringent law,” said CP Vishwas Nangre Patil.Investigators suspect the drugs travelled from Rajasthan via Ujjain for distribution among Nagpur peddlers. “Several top criminals in Nagpur were receiving MD from Phalli.
